candidate_payload_lines: The receipts-and-payments mismatch bug of 2010 — an internal note records discrepancies that vanish from the counter screen "but will still show within the back end branch account," quietly corrupting the books of some forty branches.
And in 2017, five hundred and fifty-five sub-postmasters, bankrolled by litigation funders because none of them had money left, sued the Post Office in the High Court under a single group action.
And in December 2019, Fraser handed down the judgment the Post Office had spent twenty years making sure no one would ever write.

The advice preserves it in one sentence: the emails and minutes "should be, and have been, destroyed: the word 'shredded' was conveyed to me." The thinking, as recorded, was simpler still: if it's not minuted, it's not disclosable.
On the ninth of January she announced: "I return my CBE with immediate effect." On the tenth, the Prime Minister stood up in Parliament and promised something without precedent.
Its first sentence does something no British law had ever done at this scale: "Every conviction to which this Act applies is quashed on the coming into force of this Act." Not reviewed.
In 2003, in a Hampshire village shop, sub-postmistress Jo Hamilton watched her computer invent a debt in front of her.
The screen said two thousand pounds was missing from her post-office till — money she had never seen.
In May 1998, a man named Alan Bates and his partner Suzanne Sercombe put sixty-five thousand pounds of their own money into a small post office in Craig-y-Don, on the North Wales coast.
In 1999, the Post Office began rolling out a new computer system to every branch counter in the country.
The machine was modern, the institution was centuries old, and nobody buys a village post office expecting to need a lawyer.
In Craig-y-Don, Horizon arrived in October 2000; by December, Alan Bates was staring at an unexplained hole of around six thousand pounds.
The helpline had an answer, and the answer never changed.
And here the trap closed, because of a clause most of them had never dwelt on.
In November 2003, the Post Office terminated his contract without giving a reason — its own files, disclosed years later, called him unmanageable.
What the Post Office did not know was that it had just fired the one man in Britain who would never, ever let it go.
Between 1999 and 2015, roughly seven hundred sub-postmasters were prosecuted by the Post Office itself — on average, about one a week, for a decade and a half.
Its own investigators had reported, in writing, that there was no evidence of theft.
era_note: 1999-2026, England and Wales. Village post-office counters, early-2000s beige terminals and cathode monitors, British high streets and Crown Court interiors. American police cars, badges and courtrooms read wrong.

lines.text: The Post Office helpline told sub-postmasters the same thing for years. No one else is having this problem. You are the only one.

lines.text: Husbands and wives sat up past midnight with shoeboxes of paper, checking each other's arithmetic against a machine that would not show its own.

lines.text: It was not a small lie. It was the load-bearing lie. If you are the only one, the problem must be you.

shorts.angle: The Post Office investigated, charged and prosecuted its own sub-postmasters, holding all three roles in one body about once a week for fifteen years.

lines.text: The Post Office investigated the crime, decided the charge, and prosecuted the case. Victim, detective and prosecutor, in one body.

lines.text: In England and Wales any company may bring a private prosecution. Between 1999 and 2015 the Post Office brought roughly seven hundred.

lines.text: The charge sheet carried two counts. Theft was the hammer. It meant prison, headlines, ruin. Then, quietly, came an offer.
